prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow fractional frequency uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single-part choice, and the first-round exchange has strengthened the case more than it has weakened it. The core is an experimentalist's argument. Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the dominant systematic of trapped-atom clocks by design, and the Tokyo and Boulder programmes then showed, with the blackbody, collisional and lattice light shifts measured and not merely estimated, that fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 is reachable. Independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, and groups in China) have reproduced and surpassed it, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree at that level. That is the reproducibility I ask of any measurement prize. Six of eight members now prefer this configuration, and what persuades me is not the count but that the objections raised by the sceptics (overlap with 2005 and 2012, discovery versus invention, priority outside the two names) are about framing, and none of them questions the physics or the credit of the two named laureates. On maturity, the instrument is two decades old, its systematics are understood, and the pending redefinition of the second makes recognition current. I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1; I have changed the wording of the citation, as explained in my responses, and I have replaced one alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still the one the whole committee names: precision frequency metrology was honoured in 2005 (comb) and 2012 (single-ion control, including the Al+ clock), and a strict reader can ask whether a record in precision is a discovery or invention in the statutory sense and not a refinement. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct invention, which solved a problem neither earlier prize addressed, namely interrogating many neutral atoms without perturbing the clock transition. But I accept that this answer depends on the citation being written narrowly. The remaining weaknesses are real. The applications (relativistic geodesy, constants and dark-matter bounds, SI redefinition) are mostly demonstrations and prospects, not routine use. Priority outside the two names (Lemonde and SYRTE, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemke and others) is not fully closed, and I cannot settle all of it from my own knowledge, so I would want the expert reports requested by the chair before a final vote. Finally, Katori and Ye are not equal contributors in the same respect, and a citation has to describe that fairly.

responses.point: Asks that the citation join the magic-wavelength lattice trapping and its realization in clocks, so that it is clearly distinct from the comb and ion-clock prizes, and warns that two atomic physicists agreeing is not itself persuasive.
responses.response: I accept both points. In round 1 my wording said that the clocks opened a new regime of precision in time and frequency, which is exactly the generic phrasing that blurs the line to 2005 and 2012. I now propose naming the magic-wavelength trapping and the realization of the lattice clock together, with the 1e-18 uncertainty as the evidence that it works. On your caution about our shared field, I think it is fair, so let me say what a non-specialist can check: the uncertainty budget (blackbody, lattice light shift, collisions) is published in detail by several independent groups, and the comparisons between them are public. On the share between Katori and Ye, I do not think the citation needs to rank them. The invention and the realization are one achievement that two people carried in different places, and the committee's motivation text can describe it in this way.

responses.point: Now agrees on the substance but wants the citation to rest on the invention and realization of the clock itself, leaving geodesy, dark-matter searches and the SI redefinition out of the wording because they are demonstrations and prospects, not routine use.
responses.response: I agree and I have moved on this. My round-1 citation had a clause about a new regime of precision, which was already leaning on the applications, and I withdraw that emphasis. The citation should say what was invented and demonstrated and nothing about what it may later be used for; the millimetre redshift measurement is a demonstration that the instrument works at that level, not a separate prize-level claim. On your Tokyo fellowship, I do not think it requires recusal on its own, since you report no personal tie to Katori or Ye, but that is for the chair and the committee to decide. I would however ask that my own JILA-lineage link be treated by the same standard. Both are institutional or distant, and neither involves collaboration, so I would discount neither of us, but I will not object if the committee chooses otherwise.

responses.point: Calls IceCube a strong second option, argues that the diffuse flux is secure and mature without source identification, and has not found a second part that keeps credit fair within three names.
responses.response: You have moved me part of the way. Your point that the discovery of the neutrinos does not depend on identifying sources is right, and I was putting too much weight on the thin source picture; I now see the diffuse flux as mature. That is why I replace B004 with B020 among my alternatives. My remaining objection is attribution, not science: three names out of a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND as predecessors, and I agree with you that no pairing with B030 works within a three-person limit, since Katori, Ye plus Halzen, Karle and Spiering would be five. So I do not propose a second part. If the committee later has to choose between B030 now and IceCube in a following year, I think the clean attribution argues for B030 first, and I would support IceCube once the expert report on the precursors is in.

responses.point: Keeps precision CMB mapping first but calls it the least supported candidate, concedes the WMAP versus Planck and Page versus Puget allocation problem, and says he would not be unhappy to see B030 win.
responses.response: I value the candour, and I agree that the measurement side of cosmology was left open in 2006 and 2019. My difficulty is the same one you name, with an additional point from my own side: WMAP and Planck are two missions with different instruments and teams, and a three-name trio cannot cover both without arbitrariness, whichever of Page or Puget is chosen. For an experimentalist, the instrument credit is exactly what a prize should be able to name. I do not read the low count for B055 as a verdict on its science, as most of us are not cosmologists, but I do read it as saying that this year's committee cannot defend a name set. If you want to keep B055 alive, I would ask what a reconciled trio looks like; otherwise I would be glad to have your support for B030.

responses.point: Prefers the Kardar-Zhang class, presents it as a minority view, and wants any B030 citation to name the magic-wavelength concept explicitly.
responses.response: The second half of your statement I have adopted in the citation. On Kardar-Zhang, I find the exact exponents and the liquid-crystal experiments persuasive as science, and I accept that it needs no maturity defence. My difficulty is that the 1986 paper has three authors and the omitted one, Parisi, is already a laureate, so a Kardar-Zhang prize splits the original trio, and Spohn's later exact work is a separate achievement that the committee would then have to treat on its own. I would not be uneasy about B049 as an alternative in a later year, if you can show that the experimental realizations are broad enough, but I cannot move it above a case with clean credit and many independent confirmations.

responses.point: Moved from topological insulators to the lattice clock but would not object to a new state of matter being preferred over a precision instrument, and notes that Ye worked in the Hall comb environment.
responses.response: On Ye's origin in Hall's group, which I know well because I spent time there myself, I think it makes the distinction I am drawing easier, not harder: the comb was the ruler, and the lattice clock is a different physical system that uses the ruler. I would be uncomfortable with a prize that credits Ye for the comb environment and not for the lattice work, and the narrow citation avoids that. Regarding your remark on new matter versus instrument, I agree that it is a legitimate preference for a committee to hold, but I see B058 as blocked on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, which you raised yourself, and I have not seen a three-name answer to it.

uncertainties: Whether expert reviewers find a priority claim (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or others) strong enough to change the two-name credit; I regard this as the one open point that could alter my position.

Whether the committee will accept a precision-measurement invention as an invention in the statutory sense, given 2005 and 2012, and how firmly the citation can be restricted to the lattice clock without a statement of applications.
Whether the SI redefinition, if it does happen soon, should be mentioned in the motivation and not the citation.
Whether IceCube (B020) is better recognised in a later year once the precursor-credit report is available.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA during my PhD; Jun Ye is at JILA and worked in Hall's group. This is a distant mentor-lineage link, with no collaboration, joint publication or funding tie to Ye or Katori that I know of, and I do not think it requires recusal, though I leave that judgement to the chair and the committee and I do not ask to be discounted. I also lead quantum sensing in WACQT, overlapping institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers, and hold a stake in Deep Light Vision AB; neither bears on any shortlisted candidate. I note Olsson's Tokyo fellowship and Johansson's B029 disclosure, and I have no objection to how they have been handled. No other conflict has arisen since round 1.
